command_template: python3 tools/debian_native_container_probe.py CLIENT VERIFIED_DEB DEB_SHA256 VERIFIED_SKILL_ZIP SKILL_SHA256 --fixture-mode dns-tcp-private --container-memory-mib 128 --sample-server-resources
findings: Both native clients received exact EGRESS_FORBIDDEN_ADDRESS without denied body text from the TCP-fallback private A answer, then completed approved recovery.
The TCP fixture recorded one A and one AAAA query for truncated-private.test per client; the UDP fixture recorded two hostname queries. Only two approved /plain HTTP hits occurred per client.

Both clean Debian 12 amd64 package installs/removals and 128 MiB resource checks passed without OOM. An initial exploratory run exposed a fixture bug: it closed TCP DNS after the first framed query, causing EGRESS_DNS_FAILURE; the fixture was changed to serve multiple framed queries per connection before both passing replays. No server code changed.
fixture: Route-free controlled DNS/HTTP namespace. For truncated-private.test, UDP A/AAAA replies set TC=1 with zero answers. A TCP DNS listener on fixture loopback port 53 answers A with 127.0.0.1 and AAAA with no address. Both native companion-skill workflows request approved plain GET, truncated-private GET, approved recovery GET.
limitations: No packet capture was retained for this mode. Fixture logs and code support the UDP-to-TCP/private-answer interpretation, but these runs do not independently establish DNS response bytes or every TCP connection destination.

This finite libc/resolver fallback case does not establish behavior for arbitrary DNS truncation, resolver configurations or client versions. The server ran in Debian 12 amd64 containers; native CLIs ran on Ubuntu.
Only guarded_fetch traffic in the disposable namespace was observed. Host-client traffic and traffic sent through other tools are outside scope.
